editorial:
Imagine trying to bring a tragedy from eighty years ago back to life using a special 360-degree camera. That is exactly what you see when you follow filmmaker Peter Hegedus. He wants to tell the story of Jewish women and children who were killed on the beaches of Latvia during World War II. Along the way, he meets Ethel Davies, a 90-year-old woman from Australia. Her own family was lost in that same terrible event. The movie feels like a personal journey where a young creator and an elderly survivor connect over a shared goal of making sure the world does not forget these people.

What really makes this work is the bond between Peter and Ethel. Their friendship is the heart of the film, and it keeps the story from feeling too heavy. The pacing is steady, and seeing the actual locations in Latvia gives you a real sense of place. It is a powerful look at history that stays grounded in human emotion. You should definitely check this out if you like true stories about resilience.
endingExplained: The film wraps up as Peter completes his immersive project, bringing the memories of the victims to life through technology. You see the emotional payoff when the finished work serves as a digital monument for Ethel and her family. It ends with a feeling of peace and closure, showing that while the past cannot be changed, remembering those who were lost gives them a voice and a place in the present world.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves true stories and historical documentaries.
